articles.title: Your turntable, TV and streams get one starting point
articles.dek: Search finds inputs by name, while renamed sources may need an update in Home Assistant automations.
body: Choose a speaker and Music Assistant’s new Live sources page gathers what it can play: incoming streams, line-in sources and its own TV or other wired inputs. Selecting an entry starts that source on the chosen speaker or switches the speaker to its input.

The page sits below Radio and offers list and panel views. Typing a name such as “record player” in search finds matching inputs for the selected speaker. Browse also collects live sources in one folder, and inputs belonging to speakers outside a user’s permissions stay hidden.

Names lose unnecessary repetition: the Kitchen speaker lists its own source as “Spotify Connect”, while other places can still identify which room it belongs to. Home Assistant automations that select the old “Spotify Connect (Kitchen)” name need the new name.

articles.title: Reach the Shelly controls beyond your dashboard
articles.dek: Device-side timers and configuration are accessible through an action, with sleeping devices and reset commands excluded.
body: A relay can switch itself off after 30 seconds even if Home Assistant or Wi-Fi goes down in the meantime. The new shelly.command action passes that timer to the device itself, alongside commands for schedules, configuration and status that have no dedicated dashboard control.

Shay Levy adds support for first-generation devices and newer models, returning the device’s reply for use in an automation. The accompanying guide gives tested examples for a timed switch and an automatic shutoff setting.

Direct calls require administrator access; automations and scripts retain their normal access. Sleeping devices cannot receive these commands on demand, and factory-reset and Wi-Fi-reset commands are blocked.

articles.title: Send a homemade microphone’s audio over the network
articles.dek: Up to three listeners can share the raw stream; more than one requires a board with extra memory.
body: A microphone connected to an ESP32 can supply a continuous audio stream over the local network. A new ESPHome component serves the raw sound through its web server, starting capture when the first listener connects and releasing it after the last leaves.

Each listener gets its own buffer, so one slow connection can be dropped without ending the others. Two or three listeners require enabled PSRAM—extra working memory. It is also strongly recommended for a single listener over Wi-Fi; a long wireless pause can exhaust the smaller buffer on a board without it.

The component supplies mono audio without adding noise suppression or wake-word detection. It uses plain HTTP and is intended for trusted networks. The web server’s configured authentication also protects the audio endpoints; leaving that server unprotected makes the microphone accessible to anyone who can reach the device.

articles.title: Give your Sendspin speakers a separate bass channel
articles.dek: An existing stereo pair can gain or lose a subwoofer without rebuilding its settings or queue.
body: A compatible subwoofer can join either one Sendspin speaker or a stereo pair as a single Music Assistant player. The setup dialog offers both layouts, with controls for how the bass is divided between the main speakers and the subwoofer.

The crossover—the frequency where the subwoofer takes over—can be set from 40 to 200 Hz, starting at 80 Hz. Separate controls adjust its level and accommodate a subwoofer that already handles that split itself.
If the subwoofer goes away, the main speakers play the full range again. Removing it returns it to a separate player; an existing stereo pair keeps its settings and queue.

articles.title: Keep an eye on your backup generator
articles.dek: An Enphase IQ System Controller connection adds operating state, battery thresholds and schedule status.
body: A standby generator connected through an Enphase IQ System Controller appears in Home Assistant as its own device beneath the Envoy hub. Its readings include operating state, requested mode, power rating and whether its schedule is enabled.

Arie Catsman adds eleven sensors and two status indicators, including the battery levels used to start and stop the generator and its warm-up and cool-down times. These are monitoring readings; the change does not add a start or stop control.

articles.title: Playlist transfers keep their progress through service trouble
articles.dek: The report separates missing matches, lookup errors and tracks skipped while a service asks for a wait.
body: A timeout while finding one song no longer removes that music service from every remaining match. Music Assistant’s playlist migration and import treat an isolated failure as a problem with that track, preserving the chance to match the rest.

A service that asks for a pause is held back rather than treated as permanently unusable. Long waits no longer crash the whole task or discard the matching already done. If the destination playlist was created but cannot be checked, the result says “Could not verify”.

Pär Strindevall makes a first contribution to Music Assistant’s server with the per-track handling, alongside Marcel van der Veldt’s correction for interrupted imports. A service with a login problem, an unavailable connection or three consecutive failures can still be set aside instead of repeating the same failure for hundreds of songs.

articles.title: Encrypted thermometers report again on affected ESP32 builds
articles.dek: The failure affects builds using version 6 of Espressif’s development framework; other platforms keep their existing path.
body: Xiaomi and BTHome MiThermometer messages could arrive over Bluetooth without producing any readings because the firmware’s decryption method was unavailable. ESPHome switches those components to the software method already used on other platforms.

On a classic ESP32, a test fed forty recorded messages from each of two encrypted Xiaomi thermometers into the receiver. All forty produced readings with the correction, compared with none before; messages with damaged authentication data were still rejected.

articles.title: A faulty audio packet no longer costs the whole clip
articles.dek: Skipping a bad fragment also avoids an unexpected error that can stop the surrounding automation.
body: A Reolink camera recording failed 19 seconds into a planned 30-second clip when an audio packet arrived with an out-of-order timestamp. The unfinished file remained behind, and the unexpected error also stopped the surrounding automation.

Simone Chemelli adds a check to Home Assistant’s recorder that discards these packets before writing the file. A small gap in picture or sound replaces the loss of the entire clip; a regression test reproduces the failure and verifies that recording completes.

pullRequests.title: Skip non-monotonic packets in stream recorder

articles.title: Speak to a whole floor in Croatian
articles.dek: The same language update adds fan speeds, warmer lighting, scene selection and spoken household announcements.
body: Household announcements preserve the natural word order of a Croatian message. The same expansion of Home Assistant’s Assist sentence rules adds fan-speed requests for a named fan, the current room, another room or a whole floor.

BeardedTinker also adds floor targeting for lights and other supported devices, warm-white and numeric light-temperature requests, room-specific scene commands and button presses. These are language rules for interpreting commands, rather than a new speech-recognition model.

articles.title: Correct the home’s location through a connected assistant
articles.dek: The management tools also read and change time zone, country and measurement units.
body: A connected AI assistant can compare the configured location with the place you describe and offer a correction. New system-management tools let it read and change Home Assistant’s core settings.
Paulus Schoutsen adds access to the home-wide configuration, extending the tools that already work through individual integration setup.

articles.title: Dim a wall display from an automation
articles.dek: Manual brightness, automatic adjustment and its minimum level require firmware 2.6.2 or newer.
body: A Shelly Wall Display gains a percentage brightness control and a switch for automatic adjustment. Devices that report a minimum automatic brightness also expose that setting.

Shay Levy makes manual brightness unavailable while automatic adjustment is enabled, because the display ignores manual values in that mode. The firmware requirement avoids older devices that report the brightness on a different scale; settings refresh without reloading the connection.

articles.title: Quick Settings tiles work again on Vivo phones
articles.dek: OriginOS 6 and 7 rejected the app’s controls before they could connect.
body: Tapping a tile on an affected phone could never reach its Home Assistant control. Vivo’s system interface sends a request without a detail the app’s strict matching expected; the correction makes an exception for tile services while keeping their system-only permission.
Max Baumann makes his first contribution to the Android app with the fix. Phones that send the expected request, such as Pixel devices, are unaffected.

articles.title: Volume changes reach the right Sonos Amp Multi zone
articles.dek: All four outputs share a network address, but each needs its own control connection.
body: Changing the volume or starting music in one zone could affect the first zone instead, and every zone could take that first room’s name. Music Assistant connects to each Sonos Amp Multi zone using the connection details it announces, keeping playback, volume and grouping commands attached to the intended output.
The accompanying Sonos connection library also reads each zone’s own identity. Together, the changes distinguish the four zones behind the same network address.

articles.title: Newer Platin hubs get a clear compatibility answer
articles.dek: Stereo Hub HT and Surround Hub stop retrying setup for a connection they cannot use.
body: Automatic discovery could find these newer hubs and offer to add them, only for setup to retry indefinitely. Home Assistant’s LibreSync integration identifies their unsupported LS10 hardware and explains the limitation before continuing.

The original Stereo Hub uses the older LS9 module. Alessandro Zarrilli’s correction does not add support for the newer models; it replaces a misleading setup loop with a clear error, including for entries already added.
